ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening against (i) Canadian sanctions imposed under the United Nations Act and the Special Economic Measures Act; (ii) FINTRAC/PCMLTFR identification and PEP rules; (iii) the UN Consolidated List; and (iv) as a supplementary overlay for USD-denominated transactions, the US OFAC SDN List. Enhanced due diligence (EDD) is required for foreign politically exposed persons and heads of international organizations under §61(1)(a) of the PCMLTFR, and for domestic PEPs in regulated sectors. All directors, officers, shareholders holding at least 25% of voting rights or shares in the proposed federal corporation, senior managers, and authorized representatives must undergo screening before filing of articles, and any direct or indirect control or influence by a designated person will prevent incorporation.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada – Corporations Canada Online Filing Centre (NUANS name search and federal incorporation portal)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: CBCA names must be in English, French, or both. Non-Latin scripts must be transliterated into English/French using standard schemes. The name must contain a legal element (e.g., 'Inc.', 'Corp.', 'Ltd.', 'Ltée'), must not be merely descriptive of the business or confusingly similar to an existing corporate/trademark name, and must be distinctive in Canada as evidenced by a NUANS report.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If the Director of Corporations Canada refuses a name, the applicant may submit a written reconsideration request to the Director within 30 days of the refusal notice, invoking the CBCA's name review provisions (ss.10 and 12(1)) and providing the original NUANS report and a revised statement of distinctiveness. The applicant may also elect to file a new NUANS search for an amended name. If the Director maintains the refusal, the applicant may apply to the Federal Court for a name order by way of judicial review within 30 days of the Director's decision. Name reservations may be extended by re-filing a new reservation before the original 90-day reservation expires.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: A virtual office is acceptable as the registered office of a CBCA corporation provided it uses a physical street address (not a P.O. Box), is located in the province of the registered office stated in the articles, and is accessible for service of process and production of corporate records during normal business hours. Purely mail-drop arrangements without records access or physical presence may be challenged by the CRA in tax residency and commercial substance determinations.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low (estimated 5% probability during the first fiscal year, based on the low-risk profile of wholesale botanical trading and the absence of customer-facing retail premises).

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Canada Business Corporations Act (CBCA), R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, as amended — ss. 8 (method of incorporation), 9-12 (name rules), 10 (articles of incorporation), 17 (certificate of incorporation), 19 (registered office), 24-25 (authorized share capital and consideration for issued shares), 104 (organizational meeting), 106 (first directors), 121 (appointment of officers), 128 (share certificates) and 133 (annual returns).
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Corporations Canada — Corporations Directorate, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED), Ottawa, Ontario, Canada.
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Articles of Incorporation (Form 4001) filed electronically under CBCA s. 8; Form 4002 (Registered Office and Notice of Directors) for any post-incorporation changes.
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No minimum paid-up capital is prescribed under the CBCA and no escrow account deposit is required as a condition of incorporation. Under CBCA s. 25(1), the first directors fix the consideration for subscribed shares, which may be cash, property, or past services; any paid-up capital is therefore commercially determined. A deposit of CAD 1,000-10,000 is recommended only to satisfy bank and landlord diligence requirements.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED, that the incorporators' share subscription be and is hereby accepted, and that the authorized shares of the Corporation be issued for cash to the subscribers named in the subscription schedule, in accordance with section 25(1) of the Canada Business Corporations Act; that the registered office of the Corporation be established at [address] in the Province of Ontario as stated in the articles; that the by-laws of the Corporation as presented be adopted; that [Name], [Name], and [Name] be and are hereby appointed as President, Secretary, and Treasurer respectively; that banking resolutions authorizing designated signing officers on the Corporation's accounts be approved in the form presented; and that all acts of the incorporators are hereby ratified and confirmed.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Corporations Canada — Online Filing Centre, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED).
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct a NUANS (Newly Upgraded Automated Name Search) trade-mark and corporate name search via a Certified NUANS Provider or the Corporations Canada online portal; select one proposed name; verify compliance with CBCA ss. 9-12 and the Trade-marks Act confusion rules; reserve the name for 90 days using the online name reservation module and record the NUANS reference number.
required_dossiers: Proposed corporate name (English and/or French)
NUANS search report with registered trade-mark and corporate name matches
Written consent of any person whose name or mark appears in the proposed name (if applicable)
Name reservation fee payment record (if using paper Form 4033)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the examiner queries or rejects the name for confusion, submit a written response with a modified name within the reservation period, or convert the filing to a numbered corporation (e.g., 1234567 Canada Inc.) to avoid delay.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Drafting and Execution of Articles of Incorporation (Form 4001)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Complete Form 4001 Articles of Incorporation under CBCA s. 10; adopt standard articles covering ss. 104, 110, 113, 115, 120, 125 and 126 of the CBCA or attach custom articles; fix the share classes, voting rights, and transfer restrictions; designate the city and province of the registered office; appoint one or more first directors by name and address; all incorporators must execute the articles; online filings do not require notarization or a corporate seal.
required_dossiers: Form 4001 completed and executed by all incorporators
NUANS reservation report and reference number
Custom articles or standard by-law coverage election (if applicable)
Signed consent of each first director and the occupant of the registered office address
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Respond in writing to the Corporations Canada Examination Unit within the statutory 20-day period to correct any irregularity in the articles; amend Form 4001 and refile; the original filing date is preserved once the perfection conditions are met.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Electronic Submission and Issuance of the Certificate of Incorporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Upload the executed Form 4001 together with the NUANS report; pay the CAD 200.00 (USD equivalent approximately 148.00) non-soliciting federal incorporation fee by credit card; upon approval, obtain the electronic Certificate of Incorporation containing the federal corporation number; download the certified copy for inclusion in the corporate minute book.
required_dossiers: Completed Form 4001
NUANS reservation report or reference number
Incorporation fee payment receipt
Corporation mailing address and director contact details
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the filing is queried, correct the flagged fields and resubmit within the statutory 20-day examination period; if the certificate is not issued within 10 business days, contact Corporations Canada's service standard line at 1-866-616-3404 for expedited certification.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Organizational Meeting of First Directors and First Board Resolution
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Board of first directors acting pursuant to CBCA s. 104; minute book maintained by corporate counsel or the corporate secretary.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Convene an organizational meeting of the first directors; adopt By-law No. 1 covering general corporate governance, banking, and borrowing; approve the share subscription schedule and issue share certificates to the subscribers; confirm the registered office address; appoint the President, Secretary, and Treasurer; approve the banking resolution and designate signing officers; open the corporate bank account using the Certificate of Incorporation; record all resolutions in the minute book.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Incorporation
Articles of Incorporation
Consent of each first director
Minute book, share register and form of share certificate
Corporate bank account opening package including director and officer identification
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If a first director is unable or ineligible to act, fill the vacancy by a shareholder consent resolution under CBCA s. 106(3) and promptly file Form 4002 to update the director registry.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Registered Office Confirmation, Extra-Provincial Registration and CRA Business Number
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Corporations Canada; provincial registries (e.g., ServiceOntario Companies and Personal Property Branch); Canada Revenue Agency (CRA).
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: File Form 4002 for any change to the registered office or directors within 15 days of the change; register as an extra-provincial corporation in each province of operation (e.g., Ontario Extra-Provincial Registration Statement); obtain the CRA Business Number by entering the federal corporation number in the CRA 'Register a Business' online service; open the corporate income tax, GST/HST, and payroll (RP) accounts as required; apply for municipal business licences at the operational site.
required_dossiers: Form 4002 if registered office or directors changed since incorporation
Certified copy of the Certificate of Incorporation
Provincial extra-provincial registration application form
Director identification and anticipated revenue details for CRA account registration
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If a provincial registry rejects the registration due to a name conflict, apply for an extra-provincial registration under a distinctive alternate name or obtain a declaratory order under the applicable provincial business names statute; if CRA requires reconciliation of tax accounts, file Form RC1 (Request for a Business Number and Related Accounts) to align the accounts.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Corporate Bank Account Establishment and Compliance Good Standing
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Chartered bank (Schedule I or II institution); Corporations Canada; applicable provincial corporate registry.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Open a corporate operating account at a Canadian chartered bank presenting the Certificate of Incorporation, Articles, By-law No. 1, banking resolution, and director identification; execute the authorized signatory list; request a federal Certificate of Compliance from Corporations Canada to evidence good standing; schedule the annual return filing and maintenance of the register of individuals with significant control; in parallel, commence the CFIA Safe Food for Canadians licence application for the dried goji berry herbal wholesale export activity.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Incorporation
By-law No. 1 and banking resolution
Director and officer identification documentation
Register of directors and individuals with significant control
Corporations Canada annual return confirmation
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the bank queries beneficial ownership, provide the completed CBCA register of individuals with significant control and updated directors' registers; if the annual return is delinquent, file it online with the applicable late-filing fee and obtain a fresh Certificate of Compliance.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) — Safe Food for Canadians Programme; Health Canada — Natural and Non-prescription Health Products Directorate (for herbal and natural health product components); municipal business licensing authorities where the warehouse is located.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Safe Food for Canadians Act Licence (Food Wholesale and Export category, covering handling, storage, and export of dried goji berries and herbal botanicals); where applicable, a Natural Health Products Site Licence (NHP licence under s. 6 of the Natural Health Products Regulations, SOR/2003-196).

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) — Impact Assessment Agency of Canada and administrator of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, 1999 (CEPA).
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Low-risk wholesale warehousing and repacking operation — exempt from a full federal Impact Assessment; requires registration under applicable provincial environmental activity sector registries (e.g., Ontario EASR) for refrigeration systems, wastewater connections, and organic dust control; no federal designated-project trigger under the Impact Assessment Act.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Compliance with the Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations (Fisheries Act) and applicable municipal sewer by-laws where any process wastewater or wash-water is discharged (typical limits: BOD 30 mg/L, TSS 30 mg/L, pH 6.0-9.0); volatile organic compound (VOC) releases below the National Pollutant Release Inventory 10 tonnes per year reporting threshold; fugitive dust and allergen control to maintain ambient air standards; management of refrigerants containing ozone-depleting substances and hydrofluorocarbons under the Ozone-depleting Substances and Halocarbons Regulations; no untreated organic effluent may be released to storm drains.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Fire safety and building code certification from the local fire marshal and municipal building department, including structural load inspection of racking systems in accordance with CAN/ULC-S106 and NFPA 13 sprinkler configuration; occupancy load and means-of-egress clearance under the applicable provincial building code; workplace safety clearance under the Canada Labour Code for federal undertakings or the applicable provincial Occupational Health and Safety Act (e.g., Ontario OHSA), covering forklift operator certification, fall protection, ergonomics, machine guarding, first aid kits, and emergency response plans; municipal business licence and crane or hoist periodic inspection certificates where applicable.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency / Agence du revenu du Canada (CRA/ARC), the federal tax administrator. Compliance portal: CRA My Business Account via https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency.html; Business Registration Online (BRO) service; Corporations Canada (Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada) for federal incorporation and corporate registry filings.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A federally incorporated Canadian Business Corporation automatically obtains its Business Number (BN) upon incorporation with Corporations Canada; the BN serves as the federal taxpayer identification number for the T2 corporate income tax return, GST/HST program account, payroll deductions, and customs declarations. A non-resident foreign entity carrying on business in Canada must procure a BN by filing Form RC1 (Request for a Business Number) by mail or fax, or by online enrolment through CRA's Business Registration Online (BRO) service. The GST/HST program account is identified by the two-letter suffix 'RT' appended to the 9-digit BN. GST/HST registration is mandatory once worldwide taxable supplies exceed CAD 30,000 in the current or immediately preceding four consecutive calendar quarters (the small-supplier threshold under Excise Tax Act subsection 148(1)), or where the non-resident makes taxable supplies in Canada and does not qualify for the small-supplier exception; voluntary registration is available to exporters of zero-rated goods to recover input tax credits. The same BN is also used for customs export reporting and excise purposes. A foreign-owned Canadian corporation must additionally maintain CBCA good standing, file an annual return with Corporations Canada, and obtain extra-provincial registration in any province where it carries on business.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation - A standard Business Corporation (Inc./Corp., ELF code 8615) is a separate statutory taxpayer under the federal Income Tax Act (ITA). It files a T2 Corporate Income Tax Return and pays federal corporate income tax at a 15% headline rate on taxable income earned in Canada, plus provincial/territorial corporate allocation where a permanent establishment exists. The corporation is not a pass-through vehicle: income, losses, and credits are realized and recognized at the entity level; distributions are taxed again as dividends in the hands of shareholders. This classification is consistent with the limited-liability corporate structure and the non-resident ownership allowance described in the composite key.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada has no 'check-the-box' or pass-through entity election comparable to the US LLC/Subchapter S regime. Material federal elections available to a cross-border export corporation include: (i) the election under Excise Tax Act subsection 156(1) to treat taxable supplies between closely related corporations as made for nil consideration in respect of GST/HST; (ii) the ITA subsection 85(1) rollover election for tax-deferred transfers of property to a newly formed corporation; (iii) the ITA subsection 22(1) election covering the transfer of trade accounts receivable; (iv) the ITA section 216 election permitting a non-resident to file a Part I tax return on Canadian-source property income in lieu of Part XIII withholding; (v) the ITA subsection 217(1) election for non-residents on tuition and scholarship income; (vi) hybrid-mismatch ordering rules and related elections under ITA sections 18.2 through 18.7 and the anti-hybrid regulations, which apply where an instrument or entity is classified inconsistently by Canada and a foreign jurisdiction; and (vii) capital cost allowance (CCA) elections on depreciable assets used in the export supply chain. All such elections must be made in prescribed form within statutory deadlines to be valid.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: GST/HST - Federal Goods and Services Tax (GST) at 5% plus Harmonized Sales Tax (HST) in participating provinces (Ontario 13%; Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Prince Edward Island 15%); non-participating provinces impose separate provincial retail sales taxes (Quebec QST 9.975%, British Columbia PST 7%, Saskatchewan PST 6%, Manitoba PST 7%). The federal GST/HST is administered by CRA; Revenu Quebec administers QST independently.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 in annual worldwide taxable supplies (small-supplier threshold under ETA subsection 148(1)). Registration becomes compulsory in the calendar quarter in which the threshold is exceeded. The test applies to worldwide taxable supplies of the supplier and its associates; non-residents making taxable supplies in Canada must register unless a specific small-supplier exception applies. Exporters of zero-rated goods may voluntarily register to claim full input tax credits (ITCs) on GST/HST paid on purchases and operating costs.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada does not impose a federal real-time fiscal clearance, API invoice-validation, or digital-stamping regime for GST/HST. E-invoicing is voluntary at the federal level; CRA accepts PEPPOL BIS Billing 3.0, EDI, and standard electronic invoices provided the registrant maintains complete and legible books and records under ETA section 286 for a minimum of six years. Quebec has enacted a mandatory electronic invoicing and e-reporting regime under Loi 20, with phased implementation from January 2026 through December 2028 for large enterprises; however, at the federal jurisdiction level (CA_FED), no statutory pre-clearance or digital certification of tax documents is required. Exporters must issue a valid GST/HST invoice identified by their BN and retain audit-ready records.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Exports of dried goji berries (HS heading 0813.40) and dried herbal botanicals (e.g., HS heading 1211) qualify for zero-rating under Excise Tax Act Schedule VI, Part V (section 1) when the supplier sells or delivers the goods to a non-resident purchaser, the goods are exported by or on behalf of the supplier, and title and risk of loss pass to the foreign buyer. Services consumed wholly outside Canada by a non-resident, such as cross-border sourcing, quality control, and logistics management, are zero-rated under Schedule VI, Part V (section 7). Because botanical supplement products may fall outside the domestic basic-grocery zero-rating in Schedule VI, Part III, the export zero-rating route is the authoritative position for this ISIC scope. Registered exporters simultaneously claim ITCs on GST/HST paid on inputs (freight, warehousing, broker fees, testing) in the same GST/HST return; where ITCs exceed output tax, CRA issues a cash refund. Substantiation documentation must be retained for at least six years, and a defective export claim is recharacterized as a taxable supply at 5% GST or 13-15% HST on the full invoice value.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Canadian Export Reporting System (CERS) electronic export declaration (formerly Form B13A) filed with the Canada Border Services Agency before export, evidencing the date, port of exit, HS classification, value, and exporter identification
Commercial invoice issued in English or French stating Incoterms, HS code (e.g., 0813.40 for dried goji berries), quantity, unit weight, aggregate value, and the non-resident consignee
Bill of Lading (ocean) or Air Waybill (air) showing the foreign port of discharge and an overseas consignee outside Canada
Proof-of-export evidence, including carrier cargo control documents, container freight station receipts, customs broker release records, or a Form E certificate of export where required by CRA
Inward Remittance Certificate / SWIFT wire transfer confirmation or foreign exchange record evidencing remittance of the export proceeds to the Canadian exporter's bank account

Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) phytosanitary certificate and organic certification documentation where required by the destination country for plant materials or for 'organic' marketing claims
Executed sales contract and insurance certificate evidencing transfer of title, risk of loss, payment terms, and Incoterms allocation between the Canadian seller and foreign buyer
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA audits zero-rated export claims by verifying physical export, reasonable export time, foreign consignee status, title transfer, and payment evidence. Failure to substantiate the export triggers reassessment at the applicable GST/HST rate (5% federal or 13-15% HST) on gross invoice value, accrual of default interest at the CRA prescribed rate (compound daily), and civil penalties under ETA sections 280 through 285, including the gross negligence penalty under ETA subsection 285.1 of 25% of the tax at risk where a false statement or omission is made knowingly. Criminal tax evasion under ETA section 327 is punishable on summary conviction by fines up to CAD 200,000 and imprisonment for up to two years, or both. Clawback may extend to denied input tax credits on related inputs, transfer-pricing reassessments under ITA Part XVI.1, and application of the general anti-avoidance rule (ITA section 245) where export proceeds remain outstanding for an unusually long period or the purchaser is non-arm's length. Although the federal statute does not prescribe an express repatriation deadline, CRA applies a 180-day evidentiary benchmark for foreign currency receipts; unexplained overdues invite enhanced audit scrutiny. Exporters using a non-resident exporter/in-transit procedure through a freight forwarder may also face administrative monetary penalties under the Customs Act for inaccurate export declarations.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada) issuing the free-floating Canadian dollar; FX control administration is functionally dispersed between the Minister of Finance (Exchange Fund Account), OSFI (prudential FX position risk limits for federally regulated banks), and FINTRAC (AML/CFT surveillance of cross-border wire transfers). Canada repealed its Exchange Control Act in 1951; no exchange-control statute exists today.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: CAD is fully convertible on both current and capital account; no regulatory approval, license, or central bank permit is required for capital inflows, outbound investment, trade payments, or profit repatriation. Non-resident dividend remittance is subject to Part XIII of the Income Tax Act (Canada) withholding at the statutory 25%, treaty-reduced (e.g., 10-15% under the Canada-China Income Tax Agreement; 5-15% under the Canada-US Treaty). Export sales of tangible dried goji berries and herbal botanicals are zero-rated for GST/HST under section 22 of the Excise Tax Act when the goods are physically exported, with the B/L, customs entry, and freight documents retained as proof.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None. Canada imposes no statutory surrender timeline, no mandatory conversion ratio, and no repatriation deadline for export receipts. Exporters may lawfully retain USD, CNH, or other foreign currency in foreign deposit accounts. Compliance obligations are limited to: (1) Form T1135 (Foreign Income Verification Statement) if specified foreign property exceeds CAD 100,000 aggregate cost at any time in the taxation year; (2) recognition of realized FX gains and losses in Canadian-dollar taxable income; and (3) full disclosure of foreign bank accounts in the corporate financial statements audited under ASPE or IFRS.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (Canada)
tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: RMB Settlement Account (CNH) via CIPS; North American RMB clearing hub

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Medium feasibility for payment facilitation only, with material legal constraints. Foreign digital EMIs (Wise Platform, Airwallex, Payoneer, Corpay) operating in Canada must register as money services businesses (MSBs) with FINTRAC under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act and, where providing retail payment services, must register with the Bank of Canada under the Retail Payment Activities Act (RPAA). EMIs are not Schedule I or Schedule II banks; balances held with them are not CDIC-insured, and correspondent banks frequently de-risk MSB-driven clearing flows. Recommended posture: use EMIs only as a supplementary rail for low-value wholesale receivables, while maintaining the primary operating and FX settlement accounts at a Schedule I bank.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Remote onboarding is generally permitted for a Low_Risk_Standard wholesale exporter. The PCMLTFA client identification rule requires the authorized signatory (normally a director) to produce valid government-issued photo ID; Schedule I banks accept certified true copies (notarized or commissioned for oaths) combined with a live video interview. Physical branch presence is not a statutory mandate, but banks may require an in-person activation meeting where the entity has non-resident directors, foreign UBOs, or a Hong Kong/China ownership chain. For a CBCA corporation with a majority non-resident board, the standard defense package is: notarized corporate certificate, certified passport copies, a Canadian legal opinion on CBCA director residency (at least 25% resident Canadian, or one if fewer than four directors), and the completed UBO declaration.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident beneficial owners and directors (China/Hong Kong aligned) with foreign source-of-wealth review required
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: CBCA Register of Individuals with Significant Control (ISC) filing; UBO attestation executed by corporate counsel; certified extracts from the Chinese/Hong Kong business registry; personal bank statements and tax records demonstrating lawful wealth; director resolution showing compliance with CBCA s.105(3) resident-Canadian composition.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Trade-based money laundering red flags on bulk dried goji berry shipments (invoice mispricing or transshipment through Hong Kong, Vietnam, or UAE)
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: UCP 600-compliant documentation set (commercial invoice, packing list, full-set clean on-board bill of lading, CFIA phytosanitary certificate, certificate of origin); independent customs unit-value benchmark for Lycium barbarum; third-party commodity pricing report; end-buyer purchase orders with named counterparties.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Sanctions screening hits or herbal/botanical supplement sector flagged for counterfeit claims and unregulated payment types
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Automated World-Check/Refinitiv screening output with disposition notes; Board Operating Resolution prohibiting cash and virtual-currency settlement; counterparty due diligence reports; supply agreements restricted to CFIA/FDA-registered counterparties; OECD end-use declaration for all export contracts.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Lack of corporate substance: registered office at a virtual address, no Canadian employees, no verifiable trade assets
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Physical commercial lease or warehouse service agreement; employment contracts and payroll records; utility invoices in the entity name; Safe Food for Canadians Act license issued by the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA); inventory storage and logistic agreements for dry botanical warehousing.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High deposit velocity immediately after account opening (large USD/CNH wire clusters inconsistent with a new exporter's trade cycle)
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Cash-flow forecast and trade-finance schedule; binding bulk supply or offtake agreements with named overseas buyers; directors' explanatory memorandum referencing shipment dates; ERP/accounting system showing purchase order, invoice, and shipping document matching on a line-item basis.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Compliant routing is SWIFT MT103 (USD) or Lynx RTGS (CAD) with field 70 populated as 'SHARE SUBSCRIPTION - CBCA ARTICLE 9' plus the director resolution reference number. No Bank Act or Investment Canada Act pre-approval is required for the initial equity injection below the prevailing annual WTO-investor review threshold (currently above CAD 1 billion enterprise value); an ISED notification is triggered only at that threshold for non-Canadian acquirers. Bank verification package: executed directors' resolution authorizing the share issuance, updated ISC register, shareholder subscription agreement, source-of-funds certificate from the remitting bank, and flow-of-funds schedule identifying the ultimate parent.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Primary rails: (1) SWIFT MT103 for direct T/T supplier payments to Ningxia or other herbal processors, routed through the Canadian bank's US correspondent and onward to the Chinese beneficiary bank; (2) commercial documentary Letters of Credit (UCP 600), issued at sight for high-value bulk lots, advised and negotiated through a Chinese confirming bank; (3) CAD/USD conversion at the Canadian bank's FX desk with a 1-2 week FX forward booked for settlement-date certainty; (4) CNH payments through ICBC (Canada) as the North American RMB clearing bank, using CIPS for same-day settlement; (5) domestic CAD obligations settled via Lynx RTGS for high-value items or the Automated Clearing Settlement System (ACSS)/EFT for routine disbursements. Disbursement package: commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading or airway bill, CFIA phytosanitary permits, cargo insurance certificate, and a sanctions/OECD end-use declaration.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: CAD/USD Outright FX Forward (maturity up to 12 months, extendable to 24 months) executed OTC with a Schedule I bank; no prudential restriction for a standard low-risk exporter.
CAD/CNH Deliverable FX Forward and FX Swap, available via the ICBC (Canada) RMB clearing hub, providing deliverable CNH pricing without NDF inefficiencies.
Cross-Currency Swap (CAD/USD or CAD/CNH) under a 2002 ISDA Master Agreement with Credit Support Annex, used for balance-sheet hedging of long-term trade payables.
Vanilla FX Options (CAD call / USD put and CAD call / CNH put) purchased as premia-only hedges to protect export receivables without mark-to-market liability.

Non-Deliverable Forward (NDF) referencing CNY as a residual backstop only if CNH deliverable liquidity tightens; permitted by OSFI-supervised banks but operationally disfavored for this commodity-export model.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Corporations Canada (Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days after each annual anniversary of incorporation
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: No CBCA late fee is assessed; however, persistent default on annual return filings places the corporation at risk of administrative dissolution after due notice. A reinstatement fee, revival filings and director liability exposure may follow.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due no later than six months after fiscal year-end; corporate income tax balance is generally due within two or three months after year-end depending on corporate status
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalty of 5% of unpaid tax payable plus 1% per full month up to 12 months, with arrears interest on outstanding amounts. Repeated non-filing may result in higher penalties, prosecution, and director liability.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Confirmation of Registered Office and Directors
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Must coincide with the CBCA annual return filing within the 60-day anniversary window
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Inaccurate register data may trigger an administrative notice to correct; an unresolved default contributes to strike-off risk and misinformation offence exposure under the CBCA.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: Under the Canada Business Corporations Act, an independent audit is mandatory for offering or distributing corporations. A non-offering private corporation may waive the appointment of an auditor by unanimous shareholder resolution; however, shareholders may requisition an audit or review in certain circumstances, and a court may order an audit or investigation to protect shareholders or creditors. There is no general federal asset or revenue threshold imposing audit on a closed private corporation.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: IFRS (International Financial Reporting Standards) is required for publicly accountable or distributing enterprises. A private enterprise may elect IFRS or Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE); both constitute Canadian GAAP under the CPA Canada Handbook.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: The CBCA requires every federal corporation to prepare and maintain an Individuals with Significant Control (ISC) register and to update it within 15 days after any share transfer or change in significant control. In connection with the annual CBCA return, the corporation must confirm that the ISC register is complete and accurate; all share transfers during the year must be recorded in the register of members and reflected in the annual return. Failure to maintain or update the ISC register is an offence and may result in fines and court-ordered correction.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Individuals with Significant Control (ISC)

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 100 - 350 per year for corporate registered agent and registered office services in a Canadian province such as Ontario, British Columbia or Quebec.
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 3,500 - 12,000 per year for a full independent statutory audit conducted by a licensed Canadian public accounting firm for a low-to-medium-complexity private export corporation.

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 15% federal corporate income tax rate on taxable income, before provincial/territorial abatement and general rate reductions; combined federal-provincial general rate approximately 26% to 31% depending on province of deemed permanent establishment. For the purpose of this federal dossier, the federal statutory headline rate is 15%.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Small Business Deduction (SBD) reduces the federal rate to 9% on active business income up to the annual business limit (CAD 500,000 for 2024, indexed for inflation for 2025), subject to associated corporation aggregation and taxable capital limits. Export-oriented wholesale businesses may qualify for the SBD only if the corporation is Canadian-controlled and not a specified financial institution. Provincial/territorial SBD-like reductions also apply. No federal general tax holiday is typically available for wholesale herbal import-export; specific investment tax credits (e.g., Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) and the Atlantic Investment Tax Credit may reduce effective tax, but generally not for pure commodity trading. The federal General Rate Reduction currently lowers the federal rate from 38% to 15% net of provincial abatement, and the M&P deduction is limited for non-manufacturing activities.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Form T2 Corporation Income Tax Return, filed electronically through the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) GST/HST and corporate internet filing systems, or via approved third-party EDI software; mandatory electronic filing for most corporations with gross revenues exceeding CAD 1 million.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual; fiscal period may not exceed 53 weeks; quarterly instalments of corporate income tax are required for large corporations or where prior-year tax payable exceeds CAD 3,000.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: The T2 return must be filed no later than six months after the end of the corporation's fiscal period (e.g., a December 31 year-end must be filed by June 30 of the following calendar year). Tax balances are due no later than two months after fiscal year-end for most corporations, or three months for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) with a specified business limit, unless the corporation is claiming the enhanced SBD or is a specified cooperative. Instalment payments are due monthly or quarterly as prescribed under subsection 156(1) and 157(1) of the Income Tax Act (Canada).

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Page 1 – Identification (Name, Business Number, Fiscal Period)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Legal corporate name, CRA business number (BN), corporation access code, fiscal period start and end dates, jurisdiction of incorporation, and registered office address.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident corporations carrying on business in Canada must enter the Canadian fiscal period and the Ontario or federal jurisdiction code; if the corporation is a non-resident with a permanent establishment in Canada, indicate the permanent establishment province on Schedule 4 and list the Canadian agent or branch address.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Computation of taxable income: business income, worldwide income for residents, taxable income earned in Canada for non-residents, deduction of loss carryovers, and application of federal rates and provincial abatement.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident corporation files the T2 for Canadian-source business income and must restrict the return to income attributable to the permanent establishment in Canada, applying Part I rates and the applicable provincial allocation under Schedule 5.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 1 – Federal and Provincial/Territorial Corporation Tax Calculation
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Reconciliation of base federal tax and deductions: general rate reduction, small business deduction, M&P deduction, foreign tax credits, investment tax credits, and provincial tax credits reducing Part I tax.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident corporations not entitled to the provincial abatement for provinces where no permanent establishment exists must complete the federal Schedule 5 allocation; the provincial tax credit line is limited to income allocated to a permanent establishment in a Canadian province.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Corporate assets, liabilities, equity, retained earnings, and due-to/from shareholders; includes CRA classification codes for balance sheet items.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: The balance sheet must disclose all Canadian branch assets and liabilities; intercompany balances with foreign affiliates require full identification, including the nature of the balances and any imputed interest under Section 17 or the thin capitalization rules.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Sales, cost of goods sold, gross profit, expenses (including management fees, advertising, interest, and royalties), and reconciliation of accounting income to tax income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Expenses allocated to the Canadian permanent establishment must be supported by a transfer pricing study and contemporaneous documentation; head office general and administrative expense allocations must comply with the Income Tax Act and Canada-U.S. or other applicable treaty rules.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 4 – Taxable Income Reconciliation and Loss Carryovers
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Addition to and deduction from accounting income; reconciliation of prior-year non-capital loss carryovers and capital loss balances.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: The non-resident corporation must compute Canadian-source taxable income independently; treaty relief does not permit the deduction of foreign losses against Canadian-source income unless permitted by domestic law (generally prohibited for non-residents).

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Indicates whether the corporation has foreign affiliates, controlled foreign affiliates, Form T1134 filings, and cross-border transactions requiring transfer pricing documentation.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: If the corporation has a foreign affiliate, Schedule 6 must be completed and the related Form T1134 (Information Return Relating to Controlled and Not-Controlled Foreign Affiliates) may be required within ten months of fiscal year-end.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total aggregate investment income, aggregate taxable capital, and associated corporation groups for purposes of the SBD limit and the refundable dividend tax on hand (RDTOH).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident-owned investment corporations and foreign-owned corporations must track the taxable capital limit; a Canadian-controlled private corporation status is unavailable for most non-resident controlled entities.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Claim for SR&ED expenditures, qualified property, and non-qualified property investment tax credits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident corporations rarely qualify for SR&ED unless the research and development is performed in Canada by a permanent establishment; claims must attribute to Canadian employment and resource use.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 88 – International Financial Reporting (Form T1134 disclosure summary)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: See Forms T1134, T1135 (Foreign Income Verification Statement), and T106 (Information Return of Non-Arm's Length Transactions with Non-Residents).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Form T106 must be filed for each non-arm's length transaction with a non-resident exceeding CAD 1 million in a fiscal period; T1135 must be filed by resident corporations holding specified foreign property with a cost amount over CAD 100,000.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Disclosure of transactions with non-resident non-arm's length persons and whether a transfer pricing study was prepared; attaches the summary of intercompany transactions and methodologies applied.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Complete Schedule 125 and retain the Local File / Master File documentation contemporaneously; the study must justify that the intercompany pricing is the price that an independent party would have paid under comparable circumstances.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty of 5% of the unpaid tax, plus 1% per complete month of delay for up to 12 months (with extended 10%/20% penalties for repeat non-filers); late payment statutory interest compounds daily at the prescribed rate (currently approximately 8% annually, but reset quarterly). Additional penalties for false or wilfully misleading statements equal the greater of CAD 100 and 25% of the tax sought to be evaded; gross negligence penalties of 50% for knowingly making false statements. Failure to file T106, T1134, T1135 or transfer pricing documentation attracts separate penalties of CAD 100 per day (up to CAD 2,500) per form, and transfer pricing documentation penalties of CAD 1,000 per month (up to CAD 24,000) for non-compliance with contemporaneous documentation.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: Statutory Canadian withholding tax of 25% on dividends paid by a Canadian-resident corporation to non-resident shareholders, unless reduced by an applicable income tax treaty.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke treaty relief, the beneficial owner of the dividends must file Form NR301 (with respect to the Canada-U.S. treaty) or the applicable treaty-specific waiver form with the payor, and the payor must withhold at the treaty rate or apply for a refund from the CRA. Generally, the non-resident recipient must provide a valid Certificate of Residency (Form NR73 or equivalent foreign tax residency certificate, or a U.S. Form 6166) establishing residence in the treaty country and beneficial ownership of the income. The CRA imposes a 5-year retention rule for the certification documentation, and amounts over-withheld may be claimed using Form NRA (or Form NR7-R for a refund of Part XIII tax). For dividends to a U.S. corporation, the treaty rate is 5% where the beneficial owner is a company that owns at least 10% of the voting stock throughout a 365-day period, otherwise 15%; for other treaty partners the rates vary (generally 5% or 10% for substantial shareholdings, 15% portfolio rate).
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory Part XIII withholding tax of 25% applies to cross-border royalties (including IP royalties from trademarks, patents, and know-how) and to interest payments made by a Canadian resident to non-arm's length non-residents. Under the Canada-U.S. treaty, interest is generally taxed at 0%, provided the recipient is the beneficial owner and the payments are arm's length; under many Canadian treaties, interest is taxed at 10% (or exempt for arm's length loans and certain government or export financing). Royalties under the Canada-U.S. treaty are generally taxed at 0% or 10% depending on the character of the intellectual property (industrial royalty vs. copyright or artistic royalty); for most other Canadian treaties, the royalty withholding rate is 10% (often with special source protections). Payments that are excessive or non-arm's length are subject to recharacterization under subsection 247(2), and the payor may lose the deduction and remain liable for full Part XIII withholding on the gross amount.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Mandatory contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation (a Local File and an Annual Update) is required where the total value of non-arm's length transactions with non-residents exceeds CAD 1,000,000 in a fiscal period for services or fees; for goods, inventory, and tangible property transactions the threshold is CAD 5,000,000; for loans and advances the threshold is CAD 5,000,000. A combined dollar threshold for all covered transactions is CAD 5,000,000 or CAD 10,000,000 depending on the CRA administrative guidance; in all cases, Schedule 125 seeks disclosure regardless of dollar value. CRA also requires a Master File under the OECD-aligned rules for multinational enterprises (MNE) with group revenue exceeding CAD 750 million (effective for fiscal years beginning on or after January 1, 2023, through updated country-by-country reporting rules).
approved_arm_length_methodologies: CUP, Resale Price, Cost Plus, TNMM, Profit Split
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada does not maintain a standalone general Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) statute unique to financial jurisdictions, but the GAAR (general anti-avoidance rule under subsection 245(2)) and the transfer pricing rule under subsection 247(2) impose a functional economic substance requirement: an arrangement must not be structured primarily to avoid tax without real commercial substance. For cross-border wholesale and procurement in the herbal botanicals sector, the CRA will scrutinize the location of purchase contracts, inventory risk, quality assurance functions, and decision-making authority to ensure the Canadian entity has a meaningful operational presence, employees, and premises. In addition, CRA interpretations on circular transactions and conduit entities may deny treaty benefits under a substance-over-form analysis and OECD Base Erosion Profit Shifting (BEPS) action 6 rules. The entity must demonstrate that routine procurement, logistics, and storage functions are performed in Canada by adequate staff, rather than being a low-margin agent for a foreign principal.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax Evasion and False Statement Filed with CRA
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Willful omission of cross-border sales revenue, fabrication of invoices, undisclosed offshore bank accounts, claiming false expense deductions, or knowingly completing T2 return with materially false information for the goji berry and herbal export business.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Criminal prosecution under subsection 239(1) of the Income Tax Act: fine of up to CAD 200,000 and imprisonment of up to five years, plus civil penalties under subsection 163(2) equal to 50% of tax evaded and full restitution of unpaid tax and gross negligence penalties; CRA may seize tax refunds, garnish bank accounts, and conduct criminal investigations with the RCMP and the Integrated Tax Enforcement Unit. Under the Criminal Code (R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46), money laundering and proceeds of crime charges may add additional imprisonment up to ten years.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Piercing the corporate veil under the Canada Business Corporations Act and common law: misrepresentations or fraudulent conduct by directors allow civil restitution against the estate of the company, and criminal liability may attach personally. CRA has the power to charge directors with wilful blindness and personal liability for the 50% penalty; travel bans may be imposed on Canadian resident directors when under investigation for tax evasion, and extradition treaties may be invoked for cross-border tax fraud. A director who knew or ought to have known of false filings may be personally assessed for the corporation's taxes under subsection 227.1(1) for unremitted payroll and GST/HST amounts, up to full unpaid liabilities with no limitation period for fraud.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer Pricing Non-Compliance and Penalty for Contemporaneous Documentation Failure
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to prepare or retain a Local File/Annual Update, or failing to disclose non-arm's length cross-border transactions with non-residents on Form T106 and Schedule 125, using an unrealistic mark-up rate for procurement and resale of dried goji berries, or shifting profit off-shore to an associate entity in low-tax jurisdiction without functional analysis support.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Transfer pricing penalty under subsection 247(3): CAD 1,000 per month for each complete month the documentation is insufficient or not furnished, capped at CAD 24,000 per year; no reduction of tax is allowed if the penalty applies; CRA may re-compute the arm's length price and impose consequential tax interest and 10% or 5% penalties for large corporations. In addition, penalties under section 162 for failure to file Form T106 or T1134 apply, and foreign reporting penalties for non-resident affiliate shares start at CAD 25,000 for assets above CAD 100,000.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are jointly and severally liable for the corporation's failure to withhold and remit Part XIII tax on cross-border payments under subsection 227.1(1) if they participated in the decision to underwithhold or were negligent in supervising the finance function; personal assessment for transfer pricing penalties may arise only where the taxpayer is a specified person; however, criminal exposure for conspiracy to evade tax may attach to directors who sign a misleading schedule.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company / Circular Transaction and Piercing Corporate Veil (Conduit Arrangement)
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Establishing or maintaining the Canadian entity as a shell with no employees, no local inventory, no operational risk, and no decision-making authority, with all of the dried goji berry purchase and resale activity conducted off-book from a foreign parent; or structuring circular intercompany loans that merely circulate funds without underlying commercial substance to generate deductible interest.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: CRA may disregard the shell and assess the foreign parent directly under the Canadian permanent establishment doctrine (Article 5 of the Canada-U.S. treaty and section 253 of the Income Tax Act). Taxable income is re-attributed to the beneficial owner, and the section 212.1 or subsection 84.1 rules may treat a dividend or deemed dividend with full Part XIII withholding of 25% on the entire amount; interest deductibility denied under subsection 247(2) and GAAR, plus a 10% penalty and daily interest; an entity whose core activity is merely holding assets and collecting flows is required to file a T2 return under subsection 150(1) even if it purports to be inactive; failure can trigger a failure-to-file penalty plus gross negligence penalties.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors of the shell may be personally liable for taxes withheld from non-resident shareholders and not remitted under subsection 227.1; the corporate veil will be pierced where the director knowingly creates fraudulent circular transactions, leading to personal seizure of personal bank accounts and real estate; travel bans and restraining orders may issue against directors under the financial investigation provisions of the Criminal Code, and up to 14 years of imprisonment can be imposed for laundering proceeds of tax evasion.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: AML/CFT Red Flags for Bulk Cross-Border Wire Transfers (FINTRAC Reporting)
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Conducting multiple large SWIFT TT or wire transfers with no economic reason, using layers of foreign shell intermediaries, accepting wire transfers from an overseas customer that have no connection to the invoiced goods, or intentionally splitting payments to avoid the CAD 10,000 threshold for large cash or wire reporting under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: FINTRAC administrative monetary penalties up to CAD 1 million for non-compliance with reporting and record-keeping obligations; if a financial institution files a Terrorist Property Report, the CRA may instigate a full audit; credible allegations of money laundering trigger freezing orders and forfeiture proceedings under the Criminal Code, and penalties for each failure to report a suspicious transaction or large cash transaction can reach CAD 100,000 per violation; criminal money-laundering penalities are up to CAD 500,000 and/or ten years in prison for an indictable offence.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors, officers, and compliance officers are personally subject to FINTRAC penalties where they knowingly or negligently cause the entity's failure to report; personal travel bans may attach to investigations related to the transfer of alleged proceeds, and court orders may impose civil forfeiture against personal property; the corporate veil is pierced under treaty and common law where the shell is used for a fraud on creditors, lenders, or tax authorities.
